newsitem.title: USA: S&P sees lower Calif. municipal utility ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees lower Calif. municipal utility ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said on Monday it expects to downgrade several municipal utilities in California in the near-term.
The rating agency said the lower ratings will reflect the existing cost burdens and the future operating challenges of these utilities in the context of a more competitive market.

S&P said many California public power systems have too much debt. This leaves the public utilities with the problem of how to recover their stranded costs at a time when city councils or boards of directors may be unwilling to raise rates, S&P said.

As the state and national electric industry move closer to an open market, S&P said purchased power will become cheaper, customers will have more choices, and competitors will take market share from former monopolies.
"California is moving quickly to allow these market opportunities; therefore, timely and prudent response is essential to being competitive and preserving credit quality," the rating agency said.

S&P said the Modesto Irrigation District's average rate revenue already is below the projected market rate and is well positioned to compete. The Sacramento Municipal Utility District is just above the projected market and stranded revenues are at a manageable 13 percent of expenses.

By contrast, S&P said the Los Angeles Department of Water & Power has over $450 million in potential annual stranded revenues, representing a significant 31 percent of its annual operating expenses using fiscal year 1995 as the base year.
Similarly, the stranded revenues of the public utilities for Burbank, Pasadena and Riverside account for in excess of 25 percent of their 1995 operating expenses, S&P said.

"As reflected in their rating outlooks, these utilities face the most significant pressure to implement various strategies to lower operating costs, collect revenues to pay down fixed costs, and implement marketing strategies to attract and retain customers and spread costs over a larger customer base," the rating agency said.

S&P said the negative outlooks on the five southern California municipal utilities, the Northern California Power Agency and the Intermountain Power Agency reflect its view that the California power market will not remain conducive to some of the high ratings held by public power companies.
